about: How heat became visible: when science, health, labour, finance and the UN began to notice extreme heat. Built by research/2026-11/heat-visibility/convert.js from checked research; shown on /how-heat-became-visible/.

grades.known: Original documents, peer-reviewed papers, or institutions reporting their own actions.
grades.uncertain: Its sources could not be read to confirm it, so only its year and its general point are shown.

caveats: Grades describe the evidence for what happened. Why each event mattered is historical interpretation, not a measured effect.
A claimed first is shown as claimed, with its source; no first use of an IPCC heat term is asserted.
Absence from this timeline is not evidence of inaction. Country coverage is uneven.

story.title: Heat was measurable, but institutionally scattered
story.text: Urban temperature differences had a long scientific history. This review reaches an 1833 observation through a later EPA history, rather than through the original publication.

story.title: Climate assessment gave heat a recurring policy route
story.text: The IPCC's early impacts assessments connected heat with health. By TAR, the policy summary linked heatwaves with mortality, crops, electricity and unequal vulnerability. This was recognition, rather than proof of sustained public attention.

story.title: Urban mortality made heat a public-health emergency
story.text: Chicago, Europe and Russia became reference cases for surveillance, warnings and organised prevention. The term silent describes a recognition problem: deaths can be dispersed, delayed or attributed to other conditions. It does not mean communities were unaware of heat.

story.title: South Asian experience entered both practice and science
story.text: Ahmedabad connected a deadly event with a municipal plan. Karachi followed a major emergency with a management plan. India circulated national guidance. Humid-heat research placed the Indus and Ganges agricultural regions within debates about adaptation limits.

story.title: Heat became a connected disaster and development risk
story.text: SREX connected extremes with vulnerability. GHHIN built a dedicated exchange network. The Lancet Countdown and ILO made heat exposure and lost work capacity recurring indicators. These metrics widened the conversation beyond emergency deaths.

story.title: Warming levels, attribution and physiology sharpened the stakes
story.text: SR1.5 connected temperature goals with exposure differences. Observations and experiments complicated the 35°C wet-bulb shorthand. AR6 strengthened the assessment of observed hot extremes. A 2022 India-Pakistan attribution study reached international audiences through WMO.

story.title: Institutions began naming protection functions
story.text: Examples include a heat coordination role in Dhaka North, operational workplace measures in Singapore, insurance coverage for SEWA members, and Bangladesh's clinical guidance. COP28 and the 2024 UN call gave health and extreme heat greater international visibility. Announcements, coverage and rules are different forms of progress.

story.title: Implementation, finance and regional exchange gained dedicated homes
story.text: Regional hubs in Singapore and New Delhi, a Bangladesh development assessment, city cooling initiatives and a heat-financing framework connected evidence with delivery. Maternal and child health gained more specific monitoring attention.

story.title: The transition remains uneven and incomplete
story.text: A regional history of media attention was not verified here. Disaster databases and epidemiological mortality estimates count different things. Country coverage in this review is uneven, and absence from this timeline is not evidence of inaction.

turning.title: Mortality emergencies became a prevention field
turning.text: Chicago supplied a sharply visible event and a surveillance problem. Europe supplied another large emergency. Health agencies carried lessons into operational guidance as repeated events made prevention harder to treat as a one-off response.
turning.missing: Homebound and socially isolated older people were difficult to reach. Death certification could miss indirect effects. People with disabilities and informal workers were not consistently identifiable in the records used here. The evidence base was weighted towards well-documented northern cities.

turning.title: South Asian municipal experience became transferable practice
turning.text: Ahmedabad's emergency was followed by a plan with a designated municipal health role, forecast links and public communication. Karachi's emergency led to clearer inter-agency responsibilities. Municipal bodies, health services, meteorological institutions and partners carried the work. The timing connected recent loss with the next hot season.
turning.missing: A plan's publication did not establish who could afford to stop work, reach cool space or obtain care. Small cities, informal settlements and mobile workers remain less visible in this source set. Evaluation and continuity cannot be inferred from launch dates.

turning.title: Humid heat changed the language of limits
turning.text: Theory made heat plus humidity a physiological question. South Asian projections connected it to densely populated agricultural areas. Observations and laboratory experiments then narrowed the distance between future risk and real exposure. Research institutions carried this sequence through peer-reviewed evidence.
turning.missing: A theoretical threshold did not represent the safety of older people, children, pregnant workers, people with chronic illness or workers in direct sun. Young healthy adults in controlled experiments do not represent every person or workplace. Tropical night heat and recovery conditions need separate attention.

turning.title: Heat became a recurring health and labour account
turning.text: Annual Countdown indicators, ILO projections and AR6 made exposure and work losses comparable across reporting cycles. Health researchers, labour institutions and the IPCC carried complementary evidence. This coincided with growing demand for development-relevant climate metrics.
turning.missing: Modelled work capacity is not identical to observed wages, household income or lost employment. Unpaid care, piece-rate work and the ability to take a break are not captured by one aggregate working-hours number. Women's exposure can remain hidden within household and informal activity.

turning.title: Named climate risk gained named institutional roles
turning.text: Rapid attribution connected an India-Pakistan event with climate change while the emergency remained current. Dhaka North named a coordination role; Singapore specified workplace triggers; Bangladesh issued health guidance. COP28 and the UN call carried the issue into broader policy audiences.
turning.missing: A visible role or declaration does not demonstrate staffing, budgets, enforcement or coverage. Outdoor and informal workers, children outside formal care, and people with disabilities may need delivery channels beyond alerts. Asia-wide first claims remain bounded partner claims.

turning.title: Protection became a question of income and finance
turning.text: The SEWA insurance pilot translated hot days into an income-protection instrument. The Bangladesh assessment connected heat with national development losses. UNDRR's framework distinguished financing routes for heat resilience. Worker organisations, public institutions, development finance and philanthropy carried different parts of this shift.
turning.missing: Coverage is not evidence of an adequate payout, lasting affordability or reduced exposure. Insurance cannot by itself establish safer housing, water access or working conditions. Small municipalities and unregistered workers are not demonstrated beneficiaries of every instrument.

turning.title: Regional institutions and more specific health data emerged
turning.text: The Southeast Asia and South Asia hubs gave evidence exchange a regional home. Maternal and child-health indicators added a more specific monitoring route. Yet CRED's provisional disaster table also documented delayed heat-death reporting. Networks, health agencies and disaster-data institutions carried these parallel developments.
turning.missing: Regional hubs do not establish equal national participation or local service coverage. Much of mainland and island Southeast Asia remains thin in this timeline. Small cities, humid-heat regions and groups absent from routine surveillance can remain statistically quiet even as institutional attention grows.

turningClose: Across these turning points, three changes are distinct: a hazard becomes measurable, its losses become countable, and an institution accepts a protection function. They can occur years apart. Ahmedabad's plan and Singapore's workplace measures illustrate different protection functions; neither alone establishes complete coverage.

events.title: Urban heat differences enter the scientific record
events.what: An EPA historical review traces documented city-country temperature differences to an 1833 publication. The original publication was not opened for this review.
events.why: Urban form was already recognised as a source of local heat before modern climate assessments.

events.title: IPCC is established
events.what: WMO and UNEP established the IPCC to assess climate science, impacts and response options.
events.why: Heat would gain an enduring route into intergovernmental scientific assessment.

events.title: First IPCC assessment is completed
events.what: The first IPCC assessment was completed in August 1990. Its heat-health passages could not be reopened in this review.
events.why: This established the assessment cycle through which subsequent heat evidence reached governments.

events.title: Climate convention includes human health
events.what: The UNFCCC defined adverse climate effects to include harm to human health and welfare. Article 4 also addressed public health in climate response assessment.
events.why: Health had a treaty-level connection to climate change before heat had a dedicated global policy agenda.

events.title: IPCC updates its first assessment
events.what: The 1992 impacts supplement linked urban heat islands with global warming and discussed increased mortality from heat stress.
events.why: An early assessment explicitly connected city heat exposure with climate-related health risk.

events.title: Heat deaths expose surveillance and response gaps
events.what: CDC reported 465 deaths certified as heat-related during July 11-27. It also described inconsistent death definitions and the limits of medical-examiner surveillance.
events.why: A major urban heat emergency made preventable deaths and social vulnerability visible.

events.title: IPCC names direct heat-health impacts
events.what: The Second Assessment Report linked anticipated increases in heatwave intensity and duration to additional illness and mortality. Its Working Group II summary included a dedicated human-health section.
events.why: Heat-related illness and death became explicit findings in the assessment's policy summary.

events.title: IPCC links heatwaves with unequal impacts
events.what: TAR's Working Group II summary connected projected heat extremes with mortality, crop damage, cooling demand and energy reliability. Its Human Health chapter reviewed thermal stress and adaptation.
events.why: Heat appeared as a connected health, infrastructure and equity risk.

events.title: European heatwave becomes a public-health reference point
events.what: The 2003 European heatwave caused severe health impacts and overwhelmed hospitals in France, as reviewed by WHO and WMO. Later guidance used this event to explain heat-health warning and response needs.
events.why: A large mortality emergency helped turn heat prevention into a structured public-health field.

events.title: Fourth assessment consolidates the evidence cycle
events.what: The IPCC published its Fourth Assessment Report, including a Synthesis Report. Detailed heat passages were inaccessible in this review and are listed as verification gaps.
events.why: Heat's assessment history continued within a regular science-policy cycle, although this entry makes no new heat-confidence claim.

events.title: WHO publishes heat-health action-plan guidance
events.what: WHO's EuroHEAT guidance brought warnings, public advice, health services, housing and urban planning into one prevention framework.
events.why: Protection became a planned portfolio of public actions rather than a weather advisory alone.

events.title: Russian heatwave reinforces the public-health case
events.what: The 2010 Russian heatwave became another major example in WHO-WMO guidance on severe heat-health impacts.
events.why: Repeated emergencies strengthened the case for warning systems linked to health action.

events.title: Ahmedabad heatwave prompts coordinated planning
events.what: Following a deadly May heatwave, Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation and partners began developing a coordinated response.
events.why: A South Asian city linked a local health emergency to municipal heat governance.

events.title: Theory identifies a limit to heat adaptation
events.what: A peer-reviewed study proposed sustained 35°C wet-bulb exposure as a theoretical limit under idealised conditions. This was not a general safety threshold for everyday activity.
events.why: Humid heat introduced physical limits to adaptation into climate-risk discussions.

events.title: SREX policy summary is approved
events.what: IPCC member governments approved the SREX Summary for Policymakers in Kampala. The announcement connected disaster risk management, adaptation and vulnerability.
events.why: Extreme events gained an assessment organised around risk and the capacity to cope.

events.title: SREX becomes a published assessment
events.what: The published SREX brought climate extremes, exposure, vulnerability and disaster management into a shared assessment.
events.why: It provided a bridge between physical hazard science and disaster-risk practice.

events.title: AR5 physical-science assessment is published
events.what: AR5 Working Group I assessed human contributions to temperature extremes and increasing heatwave frequency in large parts of Europe, Asia and Australia.
events.why: Observed heat trends and attribution became increasingly central to the assessment story.

events.title: Ahmedabad launches its heat action plan
events.what: The municipal corporation and partners launched a plan with health-department coordination, forecasting, alerts and public communication. WHO-WMO describe it as South Asia's first comprehensive city heat-health plan; that bounded claim is retained as claimed.
events.why: South Asian municipal experience became a reference for organised heat protection.

events.title: AR5 connects heat with work capacity
events.what: The AR5 assessment linked heat-related health risks with lost work capacity and reduced labour productivity in vulnerable populations.
events.why: Heat became more visible as a livelihood and economic risk alongside mortality.

events.title: AR5 synthesis strengthens the heat signal
events.what: AR5 judged increased heatwave frequency likely in large parts of Europe, Asia and Australia. It judged future increases in heatwave frequency and duration very likely.
events.why: Heat appeared as both an observed change and a continuing future risk.

events.title: Disaster framework centres lives, livelihoods and health
events.what: The Sendai Framework adopted targets for reducing disaster risk and losses in lives, livelihoods and health. It is an all-hazards framework, rather than a heat-specific agreement.
events.why: Heat protection could be connected to broader disaster governance and loss monitoring.

events.title: WHO and WMO integrate warnings with health action
events.what: Joint guidance covered heat-health warning-system development, epidemiology, biometeorology and risk communication. The PDF is dated 2015, while WHO's landing page is dated 2016.
events.why: Weather and health services gained a shared technical basis for heat warnings.

events.title: Severe Indian heat reinforces national planning needs
events.what: A severe heatwave affected India during the 2015 hot season. WMO's retrospective account linked the regional emergency with subsequent heat-health planning.
events.why: South Asian heat deaths became a visible reason to connect forecasts, health agencies and disaster management.

events.title: Paris Agreement establishes the adaptation goal
events.what: Article 7 established the global goal on adaptation, covering capacity, resilience and vulnerability. The opened UNFCCC workstream record confirms this institutional milestone.
events.why: Heat adaptation gained a wider international policy framework without becoming a separate treaty obligation.

events.title: Karachi emergency exposes coordination needs
events.what: The June heatwave exposed gaps in inter-agency coordination and clarity of response roles. A later management plan drew on analysis of this event.
events.why: Heat entered city disaster planning through an identified institutional gap.

events.title: India circulates national heat-action planning guidance
events.what: NDMA circulated guidance to state disaster-management agencies for preparing, implementing and evaluating heat action plans.
events.why: City experience entered a national framework for seasonal heat protection.

events.title: Global heat-health network is founded
events.what: WMO, WHO, NOAA and partners founded GHHIN. Its current history distinguishes founding in 2016 from later public launch and forum milestones.
events.why: Heat acquired a dedicated international community linking science, services and policy.

events.title: South Asian experts convene on heat and health
events.what: A South Asian workshop in Colombo discussed heat-health practice and the need for an integrated approach. The later GHHIN forum record identifies it as a precursor meeting.
events.why: South Asian practice contributed to the formation of a global heat-health exchange.

events.title: Disaster-loss inventory gains Sendai alignment
events.what: UNDRR upgraded DesInventar to DesInventar Sendai, supporting subnational disaster-loss recording.
events.why: Local loss records offered a complement to international databases that depend on event visibility and reporting thresholds.

events.title: Karachi heatwave management plan is delivered
events.what: ESSA and The Urban Unit delivered the city's management plan between November 2016 and April 2017, with CDKN support. GHHIN records city approval and a proposed evaluation framework.
events.why: The response moved from emergency experience to defined responsibilities before, during and after heat.

events.title: Humid-heat projections focus on South Asian agriculture
events.what: A modelling study projected dangerous wet-bulb extremes in densely populated agricultural regions under high future emissions. It connected hazard with poverty and exposure.
events.why: South Asia entered a prominent scientific debate about humid heat and human adaptation limits.
events.place: South Asia, including the Indus and Ganges basins

events.title: GHHIN holds its inaugural global forum
events.what: The forum had a Southeast Asian regional focus and attention to communication. Its description distinguishes the formal launch from earlier founding.
events.why: Regional experience entered a shared global heat-health agenda.

events.title: Annual indicators make heat losses trackable
events.what: The Lancet Countdown reported heat exposure and labour-capacity indicators in its annual framework, including a heat-related labour-loss estimate.
events.why: Recurring indicators made heat a continuing health-development issue beyond individual emergencies.

events.title: Half a degree becomes a protection question
events.what: UNFCCC's response to SR1.5 highlighted substantially lower severe-heatwave exposure at 1.5°C than at 2°C. The original report's detailed heat passages remained inaccessible.
events.why: Temperature goals became easier to connect with differences in human heat exposure.

events.title: ILO quantifies future heat-related working-hour losses
events.what: ILO projected that 2.2 per cent of global working hours would be lost in 2030 under its stated assumptions. Southern Asia was among the regions with the largest projected losses.
events.why: Heat became legible to labour, development and economic policy through a common work metric.

events.title: Land report connects heat with food systems
events.what: SRCCL assessed increased frequency, intensity and duration of heat-related events in most land regions with high confidence. It linked climate pressures with land degradation and food security.
events.why: Heat was embedded in land and food-system risk rather than treated only as a health emergency.

events.title: Ocean assessment expands the meaning of heat risk
events.what: AFD's official review records adoption of SROCC and its policy summary on this date. It describes assessment of ocean and cryosphere impacts, human societies and adaptation; original heat-specific wording was not reopened.
events.why: The history of heat risk widened to ocean-linked ecosystems and coastal livelihoods.

events.title: Observations reveal exceptional humid-heat episodes
events.what: A station-based study found brief, local humid-heat extremes near or above the theoretical 35°C wet-bulb benchmark. These were not evidence of sustained exposure across whole regions.
events.why: A risk often discussed as distant future became an observed, locally concentrated phenomenon.

events.title: Northwestern heatwave demonstrates rapid health surveillance
events.what: CDC reported a sharp rise in heat-related emergency-department visits in its northwestern surveillance region during the late-June heatwave, and highlighted near-real-time surveillance for guiding response.
events.why: A rare regional event showed how heat can rapidly exceed familiar health-service expectations.

events.title: Study attributes part of heat mortality to warming
events.what: A study of 732 locations in 43 countries estimated that 37.0% of warm-season heat-related deaths in its study countries were attributable to human-induced climate change during 1991-2018.
events.why: Climate attribution extended from weather hazards to observed health burdens.

events.title: AR6 raises confidence in observed hot extremes
events.what: Working Group I judged increased frequency and intensity of hot extremes across most land since the 1950s virtually certain. It assessed human-induced climate change as the main driver with high confidence.
events.why: The global heat signal and its human cause became much more firmly established.

events.title: Experiments challenge the 35°C wet-bulb shorthand
events.what: A study first published online in December 2021, with a February 2022 issue date, found uncompensable heat stress below 35°C wet-bulb in young healthy adults doing light activity. The experiments did not establish one universal safety limit.
events.why: Physiological evidence narrowed the gap between a theoretical survivability limit and real exposure risk.

events.title: Mitigation assessment recognises urban heat trade-offs
events.what: Working Group III assessed urban planning options that can reduce heat-island effects. It also noted that increased density can increase heatwave vulnerability, with high confidence.
events.why: Climate responses themselves became part of the heat-risk discussion.

events.title: AR6 connects heat with vulnerability and livelihoods
events.what: Working Group II assessed health, cities, livelihoods and Asia in dedicated chapters. The opened UNFCCC summary also presented exposure to hyperthermia from extreme heat and humidity.
events.why: Heat risk became more clearly connected to vulnerability, settlement conditions and adaptation limits.

events.title: WMO carries rapid South Asian heat attribution
events.what: WMO communicated a rapid study finding that the 2022 regional heat event was about 30 times more likely because of climate change. It also described linked health, agriculture and water impacts.
events.why: South Asian heat entered an international attribution conversation during the event's immediate aftermath.

events.title: Global Cooling Pledge is launched
events.what: The COP28 Presidency and UNEP Cool Coalition launched the Global Cooling Pledge. UNEP later described its combined cooling-emissions and access aims.
events.why: Protection from heat and the climate impacts of cooling entered a shared international initiative.

events.title: Income-protection insurance for women is announced
events.what: SEWA, Arsht-Rock and Blue Marble announced parametric extreme-heat income insurance. The announcement included premium support and design funding; it was not proof of payouts or long-term viability.
events.why: Heat protection explicitly connected women's health with the income lost when work becomes unsafe.

events.title: AR6 synthesis brings risk and equity together
events.what: The Synthesis integrated the three working groups and three special reports. UNCCD's opened record highlighted disproportionate climate impacts on vulnerable communities.
events.why: Heat entered a synthesis connecting physical risk, development conditions and unequal impacts.

events.title: Heat-insurance pilot moves into coverage
events.what: Arsht-Rock's project record dates the launch with SEWA and Blue Marble to May 2023 and reports first-year coverage for 21,000 members.
events.why: An announced financial instrument became an implemented pilot, with outcomes still distinct from coverage.

events.title: Dhaka North announces a chief heat officer
events.what: Arsht-Rock and Dhaka North announced a dedicated chief heat officer role to coordinate heat responses. The partner announcement describes it as the first in Asia; independent confirmation of that regional first was not established.
events.why: Heat gained a named coordination function in a major South Asian city.

events.title: Singapore introduces heat-stress measures for outdoor work
events.what: Measures took immediate effect and included hourly WBGT monitoring. Heavy physical work at WBGT of 32°C or higher required at least 10 minutes of hourly rest under shade.
events.why: Heat protection became an explicit employer responsibility with an operational exposure trigger.

events.title: Adaptation framework includes health and social protection
events.what: Decision 2/CMA.5 set targets covering health resilience, climate-related morbidity and mortality, and adaptive social protection. It did not establish a separate heat-finance entitlement.
events.why: Negotiated adaptation goals created policy space for health and livelihood protection from heat.

events.title: COP28 holds its inaugural Health Day
events.what: WHO recorded the inaugural Health Day and the COP28 climate-and-health declaration. The declaration is separate from negotiated COP decisions.
events.why: Health gained a dedicated and highly visible place in the COP programme.

events.title: Nepal specifies responsibilities for heat response
events.what: NDRRMA's plan assigned actions for warnings, local health teams, schools, power, workplaces and daily-wage workers. The opened English copy carries a 2024 plan year; its upload path is later.
events.why: Heat entered a multisector national response matrix in a Himalayan country.

events.title: Bangladesh launches national heat-illness guidance
events.what: DGHS, supported by UNICEF, launched national guidance with attention to children and pregnant women.
events.why: Heat response became more explicitly connected to primary care and maternal and child health.

events.title: ILO highlights chronic workplace heat exposure
events.what: ILO's Heat at work report reviewed science, policy and legislation in 21 countries. It reported that eight in ten occupational injuries from extreme heat happened outside heatwaves.
events.why: Routine hot work became visible alongside exceptional heatwave emergencies.

events.title: UN call places extreme heat across sectors
events.what: The UN Secretary-General's call addressed vulnerable people, workers, resilience through data and science, and limiting warming. WHO's account linked it with preventable heat illness and mortality.
events.why: Extreme heat became a named UN-wide action issue spanning health, work and climate.

events.title: Adaptation indicators become a shared monitoring framework
events.what: UNFCCC records adoption of 59 Belém Adaptation Indicators at CMA7. These cover adaptation more broadly and are not 59 heat indicators.
events.why: Adaptation visibility increasingly depended on measurable progress as well as declarations.

events.title: Southeast Asia heat-health hub gains public launch
events.what: Singapore's official account records the inaugural regional forum and the NUS-hosted GHHIN Southeast Asia Hub. This entry dates the public launch, rather than the earliest preparatory work.
events.why: Humid tropical heat gained a dedicated regional science-policy home.

events.title: UNEP and Brazil launch city heat initiative
events.what: UNEP and the COP30 Presidency launched Beat the Heat in Cities. Italy also pledged EUR 2 million for Global Cooling Pledge support.
events.why: Heat action gained an international implementation initiative connecting cities and sustainable cooling.

events.title: WHO-WMO issue workplace heat guidance
events.what: The agencies released technical guidance on climate change and workplace heat stress. It connected prevention with worker health, safety and locally relevant action.
events.why: Heat-health practice broadened beyond city alerts into the organisation of work.

events.title: World Bank launches heat-health and economy assessment
events.what: The report drew on climate data and a two-round 2024 household survey of more than 16,000 people. It estimated 250 million workdays lost and economic losses up to $1.78 billion in 2024.
events.why: Heat became a quantified national development and human-capital issue.

events.title: Belém health plan centres equity and implementation
events.what: WHO records the launch of the Belém Health Action Plan at COP30 Health Day. Its stated foundations included equity, climate justice and participatory governance.
events.why: The climate-health agenda moved further into adaptation delivery and the distribution of protection.

events.title: WHO updates the heat-health planning framework
events.what: WHO reports a second edition of its heat-health action-plan guidance, organised around eight core elements. Governance, financing, surveillance and review are explicit components.
events.why: A plan was framed more clearly as an operating system for sustained protection.

events.title: Disaster review makes heat-reporting delays explicit
events.what: CRED's 2025 disaster review, with a 17 March 2026 reference date, recorded zero extreme-temperature deaths in its provisional table. It explicitly said reporting delays had left many heatwave deaths uncounted.
events.why: A zero in a disaster table became a documented data gap, rather than evidence of no heat deaths.

events.title: Heat resilience gains a dedicated financing framework
events.what: UNDRR and NDMA India, with technical support from the Centre for Disaster Protection, published Financing heat resilience. It covered public budgets, concessional finance, private capital and risk-transfer instruments.
events.why: The question expanded from which heat actions exist to how different protection functions are financed.

events.title: South Asia heat-health hub is launched
events.what: GHHIN and CEEW announced a Wellcome-funded regional hub with coordinating partners spanning research, policy and public health.
events.why: South Asian evidence and local practice gained a dedicated route into regional and global exchange.

events.title: Cities special-report draft enters expert review
events.what: The European Commission's official account records review of the Cities Special Report's second-order draft from 8 May to 3 July. It gave March 2027 as the planned final release date.
events.why: Cities were receiving a dedicated assessment process, but draft material was not an approved finding.

events.title: WMO frames heat within Asian multi-hazard risk
events.what: WMO released its State of the Climate in Asia 2025 account, connecting dangerous heat, ocean warming, glaciers and early warnings.
events.why: Heat was embedded in a regional account of interacting risks to health, food, infrastructure and livelihoods.

events.title: Heat monitoring expands to mothers and children
events.what: WHO, WMO, UNICEF and UNFPA published priority indicators for monitoring heat impacts on maternal, newborn and child health. The framework links health data with heat-exposure measures.
events.why: Previously less visible outcomes gained a dedicated monitoring approach.

ipccNotes: Confidence language is kept attached to the finding it qualifies. Different reports assessed different periods, regions and definitions. A change in wording is not automatically a simple rise or fall in certainty. AR5 explicitly warns against direct comparisons in TFE.9, Table 1.

This list includes the assessment cycles and the special reports identified in the opened assessment bibliography. A bibliography verifies a report's identity and year; it does not verify its heat content. “Not yet read” means a heat passage was not accessible in this review, rather than that heat was absent.

The 1994 Technical Guidelines and later inventory/methodology reports are distinct from the assessment and special-report sequence. Their heat content was not read here. This tracker does not establish when any IPCC term first appeared.

unverified.text: Repeated access failures affected original FAR, AR4, SREX, SR1.5 and SROCC pages or PDFs. Official mirrors and summaries supported narrower entries. They did not establish every chapter, first term or confidence statement. The older special reports listed in C were identified through an opened bibliography, but their heat passages were not audited.

unverified.topic: All working groups in every cycle
unverified.text: Direct text was not obtained for every WGI, WGII, WGIII and synthesis contribution. In particular, FAR's original heat content, original AR4 heat passages, AR5 WGIII, and detailed AR6 WGII and Synthesis heat-health text remain unresolved. The table leaves these gaps visible.

unverified.topic: First IPCC use of heatwave, humid heat or wet-bulb
unverified.text: This requires a searchable full corpus and term-by-term checks, including spelling variants. No first-use date is claimed.

unverified.topic: Early heat-health records beyond urban climatology
unverified.text: The 1833 entry rests on an EPA historical account. The original was not read. Earlier military, occupational and medical heat records were not verified in primary texts.

The original landmark European attribution paper could not be confirmed in accessible full text in this review. No date, risk ratio or first claim was entered. The verified 2022 WMO account is not presented as the beginning of attribution science.

unverified.topic: Full mortality series for landmark events
unverified.text: Final totals for Europe 2003, Russia 2010 and the combined 2015 South Asian emergencies were not reconciled across studies and official records. Those totals were omitted. Chicago's 465 figure is the opened CDC report's certified-death count and period, not a definitive final excess-mortality estimate.

unverified.topic: Canadian aftermath of the 2021 northwestern heatwave
unverified.text: The opened source supports US surveillance. A verified history of subsequent Canadian warning, building or health-policy changes was not completed.

unverified.topic: Every country named in the scope
unverified.text: Dedicated plan, programme or first-institution milestones were not verified for Maldives, Myanmar, Thailand, Viet Nam, Cambodia, Lao PDR, Malaysia, Indonesia, Philippines or Timor-Leste. Bhutan appears as a regional report host, rather than through a verified domestic heat-plan milestone. Sri Lanka appears through a regional workshop. These are research gaps, not claims of absence.

The first-plan claim for Ahmedabad, first-in-Asia claim for Dhaka North's heat officer, and early insurance claims were not independently audited across all jurisdictions. Current staffing, budgets and continued operation were not established by the historical launch sources. No first national heat plan across Asia is asserted.

A primary evaluation of Ahmedabad's mortality effects was not opened and checked. Similar outcome evidence for other listed plans was not verified. Timeline launches are not treated as proven reductions in illness or deaths.
A consistent global or regional spending series separating heat from cooling, health, cities and wider adaptation was not verified. No estimate of a heat-finance gap is supplied.

Announcements and specific support are visible in opened sources, but total disbursement, additionality and reach were not reconciled. A reported COP30 health-funding commitment was not entered because its underlying announcement could not be opened and confirmed.

The opened project record establishes first-year coverage, not verified claim-level payouts, basis risk, sustained affordability or health effects. Later payout figures were not confirmed in primary records.

No comparable, reproducible South and Southeast Asian media series, Google Trends extract or multilingual coverage study was opened and verified. A study of research publications could not be confirmed either. No media-attention peak is dated here.

unverified.topic: UNDRR hazard definitions and all database revisions
unverified.text: The opened loss-statistics account and CRED report establish recording limits and delays. A version-by-version audit of heat classification, event thresholds and retrospective revisions across EM-DAT, DesInventar and national systems was not completed. Certified heat deaths, excess deaths and modelled attributable mortality remain separate measures.

unverified.topic: Complete WMO State of the Climate chronology
unverified.text: The 2026 Asian release was read. The earliest global or regional report to give heat a headline role was not established.

unverified.topic: AR7 beyond the verified review notice
unverified.text: The Cities report review is a process event. Its draft findings were not treated as approved evidence. Other AR7 material through the cut-off was not fully audited. No future report or COP outcome is included as completed.
